## Body

BLOCK — P280-001: the new contended attach wait runs on an async runtime worker

PR280 / F229; exact head ad27621c0f995aaf4cafcd9937257ebc84018c09. Static performance review, round1. pr-freeze FINAL is the prime's supplied receipt, not a freeze rerun. No builds, tests, samples, reloads, restarts or production contention injected by this seat.

## P280-001 — HIGH: runtime isolation claim is false

The production path is direct:
`PaneObserver::start` (`crates/daemon/src/pane_observer.rs:202-218`) uses `tokio::spawn`; `observe_once:247` awaits `tmux.list_panes`. The real adapter is composed directly at `crates/daemon/src/lib.rs:524-529`. `TmuxAdapter`'s async `list_panes` (`crates/tmux/src/lib.rs:870-875`) calls synchronous `stdout:469-474` -> `ControlClient::query/ask` (`crates/tmux/src/control.rs:263-305`) -> `start:343-347` -> `lock_attach:445-472` -> `std::thread::sleep:459`.

There is no async suspension or blocking-thread boundary on that path. Each10ms retry sleeps the Tokio worker polling the observer/read; a contended start can occupy it for the nominal3s wait, while also holding the shared `std::sync::Mutex<State>` (`control.rs:281,297`). Other readers, including query_live, can block additional workers acquiring that mutex. Making the caller an async function does not move this synchronous work off its executor. The new lock adds this wait to the existing synchronous handshake/reply costs; it does not create those older costs.

This is a source-proven scheduling defect in the explicitly requested contention/replacement path, not a measured whole-fleet outage. Even ordinary concurrent attach can perform10ms sleeps on a runtime worker; a slow/stopped cooperating holder lengthens it. Severity is HIGH because the requested nonblocking runtime-worker property is false and shared reader contention can delay unrelated timers/requests.

Smallest required correction: keep attach/setup's lock wait off async workers, and do not make other async readers synchronously wait on its state mutex while acquisition is in flight. Retain one-start-at-a-time, sentinel-proven setup, fail-closed flock and the existing restart/fallback answer contract. Moving a sleep to a spawned thread and synchronously joining it is NOT isolation. No broader tmux adapter rewrite or new security machinery is requested.

Named proof for the gate/correctness reviewer, not an extra run by this seat: hold the same attach lock with a cooperating process, cold-read through the real async adapter on a current-thread Tokio runtime, and keep an independent short timer running. The timer must fire before the attach wait ends; refused acquisition must launch no control client, and successful acquisition must still hold the lock through setup. Existing crash/mutex tests alone cannot establish executor responsiveness. The correctness reviewer independently confirmed the inline path and is preparing that probe; no result is claimed here.

## Worst-case cost and scaling

A second healthy process normally waits only through the first process's attach/setup sentinel, then starts its own client. The lock is released after setup, NOT held for the lifetime of the control client. Two healthy daemons therefore do not imply perpetual contention.

The requested prolonged-contention case is a cooperating holder that remains stopped/slow, or another holder preventing acquisition across retries. Each affected adapter has at most one start attempt in flight. A FULL3s lock timeout followed by5s backoff gives demand-driven timeout attempts no faster than about1/8s =0.125/s, about37.6try_lock calls/s and0.125lock-file opens/s per affected adapter. These are in-process work, not100tmux launches/s. An immediate file/lock error instead permits attempts at most about1/5s. Real delays lengthen these intervals; no reads means no attempts. Successful acquisition can additionally wait up to the existing3s handshake budget. Blocked readers' mutex wait is not covered by the3s acquisition deadline.

Every fallback-enabled read meanwhile still starts one existing tmux process. The nominal observer workload for N successfully tracked, matching-tap panes is:
-1global list_panes per observation (`pane_observer.rs:247`);
-3reads per pane per pass: show-options tap-owner (`tmux/lib.rs:598-610,1170`), display-message pane_pipe (`1172-1180`), capture-pane (`pane_observer.rs:392`, `tmux/lib.rs:1114-1123`);
- default observation interval0.6s (`core/config.rs:209`), unchanged.

Thus offered observer fallback demand is `(1+3N)/0.6 =1.667+5N` tmux launches/s per affected daemon. This is an analytic cadence/read-demand budget, NOT a measured sustained rate, a strict whole-daemon ceiling, or a prediction that all those launches complete despite the3s waits. Serial fork latency and delayed observer passes reduce achieved averages; waiting readers can produce bursts after acquisition failure.

| Tracked panes per affected daemon | Affected fallback daemons | Nominal observer-only fallback launches/s |
|---|---:|---:|
|1|1|6.667|
|42|1|211.667|
|80|1|401.667|
|80|2|803.333|

The last row requires TWO adapters falling back (e.g. both blocked by another holder); with one healthy winner and one waiter, only the waiter contributes this fallback term. For D affected daemons observing the same N panes the observer term scales D*(1.667+5N). HTTP/delivery/registration reads, stale-seat checks, repair reads and existing writes add demand beyond this table. Request-driven reads have no fixed request-rate cap here, so there is NO workload-independent global fork-rate bound. No-launch variants (query_live/list_panes_without_launch/capture_without_launch, and never-bound reaper checks) return unavailable instead of starting/forking; they must not be charged as fallback launches.

Acceptability: the timeout/backoff bounds attach effort, NOT fallback duration or total forks. The existing answer-preserving fallback is an acceptable TEMPORARY safety degradation to avoid a server crash and pane loss. Hundreds/s for a fleet-sized observer is not acceptable steady state; never describe this as0.2tmux launches/s or launch-free contention. The PR preserves the old fallback rather than introducing a new launch site; this budget is an operational limit, not a second demand to redesign that existing contract. P280-001 is the scoped blocker.

## C33/C34 and proof ceiling

C33: same-user processes are trusted. No adversarial lock-holder hardening, per-seat credentials or new authentication requirement. Slow/stopped cooperating holders and concurrent starts are enough for this scheduling/cost analysis.
C34: round1 finds; round2 checks ONLY this fix. No exhaustive mutant/fixture inventory as a gate. The required condition is ordinary async responsiveness during the new start wait; unrelated hardening is out of scope.

The attach lock is explicitly a BRAKE: removing it permits more concurrent attaches; it does not select a different outcome policy. Preserve it and destroy-unattached behavior.
